references.text: The parallel text in Matthew about the feeding of the five thousand, where Jesus takes the five loaves and two fish, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples.

The parallel text in Mark about the feeding of the five thousand, where Jesus takes the loaves and fish, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks them, and gives them to the disciples to distribute to the crowd.
The parallel text in John about the feeding of the five thousand, where Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, and distributes them to those seated there.

At the feeding of the four thousand, Jesus also takes the loaves and fish, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to the disciples who distribute them to the crowd – the same pattern as in Luke 9:16.
Mark's account of the feeding of the four thousand, where Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to the disciples to distribute, and also blesses the fish.

At the institution of the Lord's Supper, Jesus uses the same pattern of action: he takes the bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to the disciples – a Eucharistic pattern that mirrors the feeding miracle.
On the road to Emmaus, Jesus takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to the disciples – the moment of recognition that reflects the action in Luke 9:16.

Paul recounts the words of institution for the Lord's Supper where Jesus takes the bread, gives thanks, and breaks it – the same liturgical pattern of taking, blessing/giving thanks, breaking, and giving.
Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, and there is food left over – an Old Testament parallel to Jesus' feeding miracle with the loaves that were distributed and satisfied the crowd.
Samuel instructs that the food be blessed before the people eat – a parallel to how Jesus blessed the loaves and fish before distributing them.
